results.problem family: Linear combinatorial optimization over arbitrary set systems
results.bound: O(n log^2 n \cdot log|\mathcal{F}|) = \widetilde{O}(n^2) comparison queries
results.quote: For any family \(\mathcal{F}\subseteq 2^U\) and unknown weight function \(w^*:U\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\), we can solve \(argmin_{S\in\mathcal{F}}\sum_{e\in S}w_e^*\) using \(O(nlog^2n\cdot log|\mathcal{F}|)=\widetilde{O}(n^2)\) comparison queries, where n=|U|.

There is an algorithm that, for any point set \(\mathcal{P}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) with conic dimension k and unknown weights \(w^*\in\mathbb{R}^d\), returns the minimizer \(x^*=\mathrm{arg}\mathrm{min}_{x\in\mathcal{P}}\langle w^*,x\rangle\) using at most O(k\log k\log|\mathcal{P}|) comparisons.

results.bound: O(d^3 \langle\mathcal{P}\rangle) calls to the Conic-Certification Oracle
results.quote: There is a deterministic algorithm that, given access to a Conic-Certification Oracle (CCO) for a family F represented by points \(\mathcal{P}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) with bit complexity \(\langle\mathcal{P}\rangle\), finds the optimal solution \(S^*=argmin_{S\in\mathcal{F}}\langle w^*,\unknown_S\rangle\) using \(O(d^3\langle\mathcal{P}\rangle)\) calls to the CCO and separating hyperplane updates.

results.problem family: Linear combinatorial optimization with integer weights
results.quote: There is an algorithm that, for any family \(\mathcal{F}\subseteq 2^U\) and unknown integer weight vector satisfying \(|w_e^*|\le B\), sorts the feasible sets according to their weight w^*(S) (and hence solves the optimization problem) using O(nB\log(nB)) comparison queries, where n=|U|.

results.bound: poly(n,B) time; O(nB log nB) comparison queries, or O((n+C) log C) where C is the number of distinct basis weights
results.quote: Let F be the bases of a rank-k linear matroid M=(U,\mathcal{I}), represented by V\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times n} with entry representation size poly(n). For an unknown integer weight function w^* satisfying |w_e^*|\le B, we can sort the bases according to their weight w^*(S), and hence find the minimum-weight basis argmin_{S\in\mathcal{F}}w^*(S) in poly(n,B) time. The number of comparison queries required is O(nB\log nB) and more generally, O((n+C)\log C), where C=|\{w^*(S):S\in\mathcal{F}\}| is the number of distinct basis weights.

results.bound: O((n+kB) log(kB)) comparison queries, poly(n,B) time
results.quote: Using Theorem 1.5 with C=kB, we obtain an algorithm with query complexity O((n+kB)\log(kB)) and running time poly(n,B), which improves both measures when B=o(n).

results.bound: O(nB log(nB)) comparison queries, poly(n,B) time
results.quote: Using Algorithm Section 4.1.1 with the efficient separation step stated in Section 4.2.1, we obtain an algorithm with query complexity O(nB\log(nB)) and running time poly(n,B), which again improves both parameters when B=o(n).

results.bound: O((n+B) log B) comparison queries, poly(n,B) time
results.quote: we can apply Theorem 1.5 with C=2B to obtain an algorithm with query complexity O((n+B)\log B) and running time poly(n,B). This improves on previous bounds when B=o(n) and uses only valid pairwise comparisons among elements of A+B.
There is a randomized algorithm that computes the exact minimum cut of a simple graph G with high probability using \widetilde{O}(|V|) cut comparison queries and \widetilde{O}(|V|^2) time.

results.bound: O(min\{(|E|+|V|) log|V|, |V|^2\}) cut comparison queries, \widetilde{O}(|V|^2) time
results.quote: A simple unweighted graph G\notin\{K_2,\bar{K}_2,K_3,\bar{K}_3\} can be recovered using O(min\{(|E|+|V|)\log|V|,|V|^2\}) cut comparison queries and in \widetilde{O}(|V|^2) time.

results.bound: (nB)^{O(r^2 log B)} queries and time, where r is the number of distinct weighted degrees; (nB)^{O(log B)} for degree-regular graphs
results.quote: For a graph G=(V,E) with unknown integer edge weights in the range [0,B], the minimum cut can be found using (nB)^{O(r^2\log B)} queries and time, where r=|\partial_w(u):u\in V| is the number of distinct weighted degrees among all vertices. In the special case of degree-regular graphs, the complexity is (nB)^{O(\log B)}.

results.bound: O(n log n) comparison queries, \widetilde{O}(n^2) time
results.quote: the minimum-weight basis of a matroid on n elements can be found O(n\log n) comparison queries in \widetilde{O}(n^2) time
the minimum-weight set in the intersection of two matroids on an n-element ground set can be found using O(n^4) comparison queries/time
the minimum-length s-t path in a graph (or a negative cycle, if one exists) can be found using using O(n^3) walk comparisons in O(n^3) time.

results.bound: polynomial-time algorithm using only comparisons between perfect matchings
results.quote: There is a polynomial-time algorithm to find the minimum-weight perfect matching in a complete bipartite graph K_{n,n} using only comparisons between perfect matchings.

results.problem family: Linear combinatorial optimization with integer weights
results.bound: O((n+C) log C) comparison queries where C is the number of distinct weight values
results.quote: In fact, the number of comparison queries required is O((n+C)\log C) if C is the number of distinct weight values realized by the feasible set.
